prompt.context: Big Green Fuel Systems, a large provider of fuel additives required for the production of gasoline, has recently developed a substantially improved form of ethanol that adds 20% efficiency (measured as miles driven on a single gallon of ethanol). This version of fuel is costly to produce but the market is large and growing more rapidly as increased amounts of ethanol are being used in fuel blends. The company has engaged your team to help determine the viability of this new product, and, if it is viable, how to go about the process of launching it.
prompt.question: Determine the viability of Big Green's new high-efficiency ethanol product and, if viable, recommend how to launch it.

clarifying_info.q: Is the company working in the US only?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, please concentrate on the US market only.

clarifying_info.q: Does the current infrastructure exist to make and support this product?
clarifying_info.a: It is compatible with other infrastructure in the external value chain, but Big Green does not yet have the capacity to mass produce it.

clarifying_info.q: What criteria does Big Green want us to use to determine the viability of the project?
What is the value chain for this product from Big Green to the consumer?
clarifying_info.a: Ethanol is delivered from manufacturers to fuel blenders, who then sell and deliver in bulk to filling stations, who in turn sell it to consumers.

clarifying_info.q: Does Big Green have a patent on this technology?

framework: Standard valuation: assess ROI including initial and recurring investment vs. incremental profit from the venture
Intangible benefits: positive PR, spin-offs, brand positioning beyond the direct sale of ethanol
Barriers to launch: internal capability gaps (Big Green lacks mass-production capacity) and external pressures across the value chain
Value to other parties: standalone value for Big Green vs. licensing/selling to another more capable producer
Competitive response: how existing competitors will react and how that ripples through the full value chain

questions.prompt: Size the US market for ethanol in gallons. Use the following data: two blends exist — E-85 (85% ethanol, 10% of the market) and E-15 (15% ethanol, 90% of the market). Total US miles driven last year: 1,800 billion miles. You will need to ask for one additional data point to complete the calculation.
questions.guidance: The candidate must recognize that average fuel economy is missing and ask for it. The interviewer provides 20 mpg. Then apply: gallons of ethanol = (total miles / mpg) * ethanol% * market share for each blend, summed across both blends. The candidate should note the large, highly fragmented market after computing the result.

math.setup: Gallons of ethanol = (1,800B miles / 20 mpg) * 85% * 10% + (1,800B miles / 20 mpg) * 15% * 90%
math.answer: ~19.8 billion gallons of ethanol per year

questions.prompt: Assume the analysis has determined there is no net savings from using the new fuel — development and delivery costs exactly offset the revenue that can be gained. The CEO has nonetheless committed to launching it. How would you appeal to each level of the value chain to promote this product?
questions.guidance: Candidate should walk the full value chain from blenders to filling stations to consumers, articulating a distinct value proposition at each level. Key points: Blenders — use 20% less ethanol per blend (efficiency), differentiate competitively, reduce distribution costs, and position ahead of potential future regulation. Filling stations — differentiation for eco-sensitive consumers, positive PR, fewer refills needed from blenders reducing delivery costs, potential to operate from smaller tanks enabling new locations. Consumers — eco-friendliness appeal, higher per-unit cost offset by fewer fill-ups needed (net cost neutral or better on a per-mile basis), and time savings at the pump.

recommendation: Given the CEO's commitment to launch, Big Green should proceed with the rollout of the new high-efficiency ethanol.

Appeal to blenders on the basis of reduced delivery costs (blending 20% less) and competitive differentiation; appeal to filling stations on eco-friendly positioning and reduced restocking frequency; appeal to consumers on environmental benefits and fewer required fill-ups.
risks: Higher per-fill cost creates a price-perception problem with consumers — even though per-mile cost is similar or better, consumers may resist paying more at the pump.
Marketing spend to counter negative price perception could erode already thin margins.
New fuel formulation may be more corrosive than existing fuels, creating product liability and infrastructure compatibility risks.
next_steps: Launch a regional pilot program paired with targeted marketing to test fuel efficacy, consumer acceptance, and value chain response.
Apply lessons learned from the pilot to a gradual national roll-out, adjusting messaging and pricing strategy as needed.
